anchors: South Sea Company: chartered 1711 as a public-private monopoly on trade with Spanish South America in exchange for converting government annuity debt into company shares.
The 1719-1720 debt-for-equity conversion scheme: holders of government annuities could exchange them for South Sea stock; the share price rose roughly tenfold in 1720 before the September crash.

The Bubble Act (June 1720) restricted rival joint-stock promotion, concentrating speculation in South Sea stock; the 1721 Commons inquiry documented bribery of ministers and MPs via stock ledger entries.
Robert Walpole survived the scandal; his 1721-1722 rise to lead the government was consolidated by his handling of the resolution — the episode was known as the Screen.
The citations for this dossier are the South Sea Company entity and the 1807-1820 winding-up Acts; the scandal and inquiry records are the historical context, not cited as case law.
East India Company: private joint-stock company with monopoly on trade east of the Cape; after Plassey (1757) it collected the revenue (diwani) of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa.
The Bengal famine of 1770 is estimated in contemporaneous Company and Indian sources to have killed roughly a third of the population of the affected provinces.
The Company continued land-tax collection at high fixed demand during the famine years, and the price of rice and other grains rose dramatically in 1769-1770.

The 1773 Regulating Act and the Tea Act followed: Parliament tightened control over the Company, granted a 1.4 million pound loan to relieve its debts, and left its monopoly intact - the loan was repaid through continued Bengal revenue.
The 1784 India Act further subordinated the Company to a parliamentary Board of Control - the famine and the companys insolvency were cited as causes of the reform.
Nathan Mayer Rothschild: head of the London branch of the family bank, the leading financier of the British war effort against Napoleon after 1813.

The traditional account: Rothschild had advance news of Napoleons defeat at Waterloo (June 18 1815) via courier or channel, and profited on the London Stock Exchange - the details of the exact channel and the extent of any exclusivity are disputed and were not contemporaneously documented.

The verifiable core: Rothschilds agents and correspondents gave him faster news of Napoleons return and defeat than the government had, and the Rothschild network financed the post-war adjustment of British government securities.

After Waterloo the Rothschild brothers (London and Paris) dominated government loan issuance across Europe; their first major operation was financing the French indemnity payment to the Allied powers.

The courier legend became a durable viral story about insider advantage at the heart of modern finance; the documented record is of a family bank that built a private intelligence network faster than the governments of Europe.

The Great Irish Famine (1845–52) collapsed Irish rents and land values; the potato failures of 1845–49 killed on the order of a million people and drove mass emigration, while landlords’ rental income failed and their encumbrances — mortgages and judgement debts, owed largely to English and London lenders — remained fixed.

The Encumbered Estates Act 1849 (passed August 1849) established the Encumbered Estates Court with power to sell encumbered Irish estates quickly, overriding prior judicial and settlement constraints on sale, and to pay the proceeds to creditors ahead of other interests.

The court sat from 1849–50; sales began in 1850, and estates fetched famine-depression prices far below pre-famine values. On the order of three thousand estates had been sold by the time the court was superseded — a widely cited figure in the scholarship.

The Landed Estates Court (Ireland) Act 1858 (21 & 22 Vict. c. 72) replaced the Encumbered Estates Court with the Landed Estates Court, retaining and extending the same liquidation machinery; further acts in 1861 and 1866 amended it, and the court’s jurisdiction passed to the High Court of Justice in Ireland in the late 1870s.

The transfer changed the owners, not the terms of tenure: tenant farmers gained no security from the sales, eviction-driven clearance continued, and the creditors’ liquidation that sold the land while leaving tenancy untouched is documented in scholarship as presaging the land-question politics of the 1870s–80s (Land League, 1879 onward).

The 1858 parliamentary record preserves the transfer debate: an 1858 Commons supply debate records commissioners of the Encumbered Estates Court and a Land Transfer Office being accommodated in new law buildings, and the same session’s Commons committee debate on the Sale and Transfer of Land (Ireland) Bill records the parliamentary-title principle argued for encumbered estates sold under the machinery.

A parliamentary notice of the 1858 transfer states that the Transfer of Land Bill extended the powers hitherto exercised by the Incumbered Estates Commissioners and facilitated an indefeasible title for purchasers of land — contemporary record that the 1858 act carried the 1849 court’s liquidation machinery forward under its period spelling.

In the 11 May 1858 Lords third-reading debate on the bill, Lord Cranworth framed the measure as following the Royal Commission’s report on the Irish encumbered estates courts, and Lord St Leonards stated on the record that Sir Robert Peel had authored the original Incumbered Estates Act — speakers’ claims preserved in Hansard, not census figures.
Samuel Plimsoll (1824-1898): English coal merchant turned MP for Derby, campaigner against overloaded ships.
The British Merchant Shipping (Load Line) Act 1876 mandated a load line marking the maximum safe draught - the Plimsoll line - on British vessels.
Plimsoll exposed shipowners who overloaded, insured heavily, and collected on sinkings; the phrase coffin ships was used for the practice.
Plimsoll was briefly suspended from the Commons for disorderly protest against the watered-down bills before the 1876 Act passed.
The load line became universal standard practice in merchant shipping; the mechanism is the industry profiting from loss of life (coffin ships) versus the marking that limited it.

The panic of May 1893 forced receiverships on a wave of American railroads; contemporary counts put more than 70 roads in receivership by 1895, among them Atchison Topeka & Santa Fe, Union Pacific, Northern Pacific, Philadelphia & Reading and the Erie.

Receivers were appointed by courts of equity, typically on application of creditors or friendly interests; the same financial houses that had underwritten the roads' securities supplied the receivers and dominated the reorganization committees.

The receivership kept the road operating and routed income to fixed charges, while reorganization committees marshalled junior security holders into depositing securities under threat of exclusion from the reorganized company — a practice contemporaries called "friendly receivership".

Reorganizations closed via foreclosure sales conveying the properties to new companies organized by the same interests; the wave drew sustained criticism and helped drive later railroad reorganization reform (culminating in Section 77, 1933).
The citations for this dossier are CourtListener records of a later (1912) Washington Supreme Court receivership opinion; the 1893-95 wave is the historical context, not the litigated case.

Nikola Tesla, financed by J. P. Morgan, began in 1901 to build a plant at Wardenclyffe (Shoreham, Long Island) intended for transatlantic wireless communication and, per Tesla's plans, ultimately global power transmission.
Morgan had committed $150,000; the plant was unfinished when Marconi's transatlantic signal (December 1901) demonstrated wireless telegraphy on far less capital.
Morgan declined further funding; Tesla mortgaged and lost the property, and the tower was demolished in 1917.
The lore — Morgan withdrawing upon asking "where do we put the meter?" — is not documented; the documented record is the withdrawal of funding after a competitor's success and the loss of the plant.
The United States Supreme Court in 1943 (Marconi Wireless Telegraph Co. v. United States, 320 U.S. 1) held that Tesla's prior patents anticipated parts of Marconi's patent.
The Aldrich–Vreeland Act of May 1908, passed after the Panic of 1907, created the National Monetary Commission chaired by Senator Nelson W. Aldrich of Rhode Island.
The commission toured Europe and issued its reports 1910–1912; its findings informed the Aldrich Plan for a National Reserve Association with 15 district associations under banker-dominated boards.

In November 1910 Aldrich met a small group of banking figures at the Jekyll Island Club, Georgia, to draft the reserve plan — established by later accounts of participants, later itself framed by conspiracy writing as a secret cabal.
The Aldrich Plan was rejected in Congress and attacked in the 1912 campaign as a "money trust" instrument; Woodrow Wilson ran against it.
The Federal Reserve Act of December 1913 created the Federal Reserve System — a compromise adopting the reserve-association architecture but placing a public presidentially appointed Board over it.
Titanic: White Star Line steamer, sank April 15 1912 after striking an iceberg on her maiden voyage; about 1,500 of roughly 2,200 aboard died.

The steerage/third-class passenger death toll was proportionally far higher than first class; contemporary reports and later inquiries cited locked gates and passageway arrangements that hindered third-class access to the boat deck.

The 1912-1913 US Senate inquiry (Smith Committee) and the British Wreck Commissioner inquiry (Mersey) investigated the loss; the Mersey inquiry has been criticized as a whitewash for its focus on crew conduct over company policy.
J. Bruce Ismay, managing director of the White Star Lines parent company, survived the sinking and was widely condemned for leaving in a collapsible boat; the British inquiry declined to censure him.
The disaster produced the 1913-1914 SOLAS convention mandating lifeboat capacity for all aboard - the first major international maritime safety treaty.

On April 15, 1912, the first wireless bulletins relayed via shore stations and press associations reported the Titanic safe, in tow, all passengers saved; Halifax papers ran the false report the morning of April 16.

The false dispatches traced to garbled relay traffic: wireless was a private commercial service (Marconi Company operators aboard ships) whose messages outran official confirmation; neither the White Star Line nor the government had a faster channel of its own.
The fog persisted for hours; the first accurate passenger lists came only when the Carpathia docked in New York (April 18).

The episode is a founding case of information fog in a mass-market event: the private information infrastructure produced the news, and the error corrected only when slower official channels caught up.
The Marconi scandal (1912-1913): British political scandal over insider dealing in shares of the Marconi Wireless Telegraph Company.
In March 1912 the British Post Office awarded the Marconi Company a contract for the Imperial wireless chain - the contract was awarded without competitive tender and was criticized in Parliament.

Postmaster-General Herbert Samuel and other senior Liberal ministers or their associates had purchased Marconi shares before or during the award; the accusation of insider dealing drove a major parliamentary investigation.
Godfrey Isaacs (Marconi managing director, brother of Rufus Isaacs the Attorney-General who also bought shares) was central; the Isaacs family share purchases were documented by the inquiry.

The parliamentary inquiry (1913) cleared the ministers of corruption but the scandal damaged the Liberal government; the affair became a durable precedent in British political discourse for the appearance of insider dealing.
Benjamin Strong was Governor (then styled Governor, later President) of the Federal Reserve Bank of New York from its founding in November 1914 until his death in October 1928.

Montagu Norman was Governor of the Bank of England 1920–1944; the Strong–Norman working partnership, including shared views on gold-sterilisation and market management, is documented in scholarship and the FRBNY archives.
At the July 1927 conference on Long Island, Strong, Norman, Rist and Schacht agreed to ease — a decision later identified (contested) as feeding the late-1920s speculation.

The New York call-loan market financed stock margin purchases; broker loans roughly doubled 1927–1929 and non-bank lenders ("others") supplied most of the growth — all documented in Federal Reserve and NYSE data of the period.
Strong’s death in October 1928 removed the transatlantic coordination; whether the NY Fed alone could manage the call-rate structure was the live question through the 1929 break.
Operation Ajax (TPAJAX): the CIA/MI6-organized coup of August 19, 1953 that deposed Iranian Prime Minister Mohammad Mossadegh and restored the Shah to full authority.

Context: the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company refinery at Abadan — Britain's single largest overseas asset — was nationalized by Iran in March 1951; a British embargo and closure of the refinery followed, and Mossadegh moved toward the Soviet bloc as negotiations failed.
The coup plan used hired crowds, staged disorder and a royal decree dismissing Mossadegh; the first attempt failed on August 16 and the operation succeeded on August 19.

The CIA's own internal history of the operation, released in part since 2000, and the Agency's 2013 acknowledgment, document the Agency's organizing role: regime change as a remedy for the nationalization of an extraction concession.

Operation PBSuccess, the CIA-directed operation that overthrew Guatemala’s elected president Jacobo Árbenz in June 1954, is officially documented in the CIA’s own declassified history (Nick Cullather, 1994).

Árbenz’s Decree 900 (1952) redistributed unused land, including United Fruit Company holdings, with compensation pegged to the company’s own declared tax valuations — far below market — which became the core dispute.

United Fruit Company lobbied Washington intensively; the Dulles brothers’ connections to the company (Sullivan & Cromwell had represented UFC, and both brothers held UFC-linked interests) are documented in scholarship.
The March 1953 arms purchase from Czechoslovakia, and the resulting "communist penetration" framing, supplied the immediate justification used in PBSuccess planning (1952–53).
Carlos Castillo Armas became president after the coup; UFC lands were largely returned, and decades of civil conflict followed — the ledger outcome the operation purchased.
The 1973–74 oil embargo roughly quadrupled the oil price; Saudi Arabia and other OPEC members accumulated large dollar surpluses with nowhere established to put them.

Treasury Secretary William E. Simon led the 1974 Saudi negotiations that opened US Treasury purchases to the Saudis; the arrangement was secret at the time and reconstructed decades later from released official files and Simon’s own memoirs.
The US-Saudi Joint Commission on Economic Cooperation (June 1974) institutionalised the financial and military relationship.

The documented mechanism is surplus recycling through Treasuries and oil priced in dollars; the strong "secret treaty binding oil to the dollar" version is unsupported and must be separated from the documented recycling.
The result locked in structural US fiscal capacity through the decade — OPEC surpluses became a standing bid under US debt, the ledger line the mechanism belongs on.
Banco Ambrosiano: Milan private bank known as the bankers' bank of the Vatican; its 1982 collapse (roughly $1.2-1.4bn in missing/phantom loans) was then Italy's largest banking failure.

Roberto Calvi: chairman of Banco Ambrosiano, nicknamed 'God's Banker' for the Vatican's IOR shareholding and shell-company network; found dead, hanging under Blackfriars Bridge, London, June 18 1982 — days after fleeing a conviction for currency violations.
Propaganda Due (P2): covert Masonic lodge led by Licio Gelli whose member list (discovered in 1981 raids) included politicians, bankers and officials; Gelli was a fugitive in South America in 1982.
The Vatican's IOR (Institute for the Works of Religion) held an interest in Ambrosiano and was pressured into a settlement of roughly $250m for creditors after Calvi's death.

Calvi's death was first ruled suicide by a London coroner's inquest; later Italian investigations and a second inquest concluded murder, and in 2005-2007 defendants including Giuseppe Calo and Flavio Carboni were acquitted of the murder at Rome trials.
LOGCAP (Logistics Civil Augmentation Program), launched by the US Army in 1985, pre-awards contingency logistics contracts so contractors support military operations without new wartime procurement.
Brown & Root (later Halliburton subsidiary KBR; separated as KBR Inc in 2007) won LOGCAP I (1992, Balkans support) and LOGCAP III (December 2001, covering Kuwait, Afghanistan and Iraq).
LOGCAP III work was awarded on a cost-plus award-fee basis — the fee structure congressional investigators later scrutinised.

Documented in GAO and DoD-IG reports and congressional hearings: KBR fuel-import pricing (2003–04), dining-facility cost claims (2004–05), and the electrocution deaths of US soldiers in KBR-built showers (DoD-IG 2009).

Dick Cheney was Halliburton CEO 1995–2000; his deferred compensation from the company continued into his vice presidency — publicly documented, and publicly attacked as a conflict of interest, the framing this node must keep exact.
In-Q-Tel: a non-profit strategic investment vehicle chartered in 1999 by the CIA to fund commercial data technologies useful to the intelligence community.

Palantir Technologies was founded in 2003 by Peter Thiel, Alex Karp and others, with early investment from Thiel's Founders Fund and, as widely reported, In-Q-Tel; its first customers were intelligence and defense agencies.
Palantir's Gotham platform was built for government integration of fragmented data; documented early contracts include FBI, CIA and Department of Defense entities.

The structure: public-purpose venture capital incubates a private data-integration champion; the intelligence community is the first customer, then the product rolls out to immigration enforcement, police and commercial clients.

Team Themis: a contractor group — Palantir, Berico Technologies and HBGary Federal — assembled late 2010 by the law firm Hunton & Williams (counsel to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce and Bank of America) to propose counter-campaigns against the Chamber's and the bank's perceived opponents.

The proposals (exposed February 2011 after Anonymous compromised HBGary Federal) suggested infiltration, surveillance and disinformation targeting critics of the Chamber and supporters of WikiLeaks, including named journalists and a union.
Palantir and Berico severed ties with HBGary; Palantir suspended the employee involved, its CEO apologized publicly, and no contracts were pursued; members of Congress sent letters of inquiry.

The mechanism the dossier documents: the same data-integration platform sold to the security state proposed, in writing, for domestic counter-surveillance of political opponents — the proposal that surfaced is evidence of the intent, not of any executed operation.

Palantir USG holds a Department of Defense enterprise agreement (IDIQ W519TC-25-D-0039); the cited 2025-26 task orders (field service representatives, Maven Smart System, SETAF combat assessment, APAS renewal) are drawn from that ledger.

Public reporting (2022-2025) documents Palantir's Immigration Operating System contract with ICE — reported near $30 million — and ICE's growing dependence on Palantir tools since the 2014 ICANTS system.

The citations for this dossier document Palantir's federal award ledger and SEC filings; the ICE ImmigrationOS contract is established by public reporting, NOT by these ledger rows — the dossier must say so.

Conservative language is mandatory for the ICE relationship; the documented mechanism is a data-integration vendor rolling the same platform across defense and immigration enforcement, so one side of the house funds the capabilities the other side deploys.

Commissioner Lin Zexu confiscated and destroyed 20,283 chests of British-owned opium at Canton in 1839; Superintendent Charles Elliot had told the traders the Crown would make good their loss, converting a private contraband stock into a claim on the British Treasury.

The Treaty of Nanking (29 August 1842) made the Chinese state pay that claim: Art. IV, six million dollars for the surrendered opium; Art. V, three million for Hong-merchant debts; Art. VI, twelve million for the expedition’s costs; Art. VII, twenty-one million dollars in all, on a schedule running to 1845, plus the cession of Hong Kong and five treaty ports.
Sir James Graham’s censure motion of 7 April 1840 put the war to a three-night Commons debate (HC Deb 07 April 1840 vol 53 cc669-748); it was defeated 271 to 262, and the expedition sailed.

Jardine, Matheson & Co. and Dent & Co. were the largest holders of the surrendered opium; William Jardine lobbied Palmerston in London through 1839-40 and supplied the war plan and the indemnity demand that the treaty substantially followed.
Be conservative about attributions of motive to named individuals; the documented ledger is the treaty text and the Commons division, not private intent.

The War Department paid steamboat operators a per-head bounty to carry released Union prisoners north from Vicksburg in spring 1865 — five dollars an officer, ten dollars an enlisted man — which made a human payload the most valuable freight on the river.
The Sultana was licensed for 376 passengers and left Vicksburg with roughly 2,100-2,400 aboard, most of them parolees from Cahaba and Andersonville.

A boiler sprang a leak at Vicksburg; the boilermaker advised replacing the bulged sheets, and the repair actually made was a patch, because a days-long repair would have handed the payload to a rival boat.
The boilers exploded above Memphis about 2 a.m. on 27 April 1865. Estimates of the dead run from about 1,100 to 1,800; it remains the deadliest maritime disaster in United States history.

Captain J. Cass Mason died in the explosion. Captain Frederic Speed was court-martialled and convicted; the Judge Advocate General disapproved the verdict and it was annulled. Chief quartermaster Reuben Hatch, the officer suspected of the kickback, never appeared. Nobody was punished.
The disaster competed for news with Lincoln’s assassination (14 April) and the killing of John Wilkes Booth (26 April) and was effectively buried.

Carnegie Steel’s chairman Henry Clay Frick locked out the Amalgamated Association at Homestead in July 1892 and contracted the Pinkerton National Detective Agency to deliver about 300 armed men by barge; the 6 July landing became a gun battle that killed men on both sides, and the Pennsylvania militia then occupied the town.

Three congressional investigations followed: the House Judiciary Committee’s hearings (H. Misc. Doc. 52-335), its report of 7 February 1893 (H. Rept. 52-2447), and a Senate select committee moved by Senator Hansbrough from the Committee on Education and Labor (S. Rept. 52-1105, 1 August 1892).

The statutory answer was the Anti-Pinkerton proviso carried in the sundry civil appropriations act of 3 March 1893 (27 Stat. 591, now 5 U.S.C. 3108): the federal government may not employ a Pinkerton employee or a similar organization. It binds federal hiring only — it says nothing about a private corporation hiring an armed agency against its own workforce.
Prosecutions arising from Homestead — including treason charges against strike leaders — produced no convictions on either side.
Be precise that the congressional records are investigations and a report, not a judgment of liability.

queries.q: Final report of the Commission on Industrial Relations

anchors: The United Mine Workers struck Colorado Fuel & Iron — controlled by the Rockefeller interests — in September 1913; evicted miners and their families moved into tent colonies on leased ground, the largest at Ludlow.

Company-paid guards and the Colorado National Guard faced the colonies through the winter. On 20 April 1914 the Ludlow colony was fired on and burned; about twenty people died, including two women and eleven children who suffocated in a pit dug beneath a tent.

Two federal inquiries took evidence: the House Committee on Mines and Mining under House Resolution 387, and the U.S. Commission on Industrial Relations, which examined John D. Rockefeller Jr. in 1915 and published George P. West’s Report on the Colorado Strike; the Commission’s final report was filed as H. Rept. 64-31 on 11 January 1916.
Militia officers tried by court-martial were acquitted; no one was convicted over the deaths.

The company’s answer was the Colorado Industrial Plan — an employee-representation scheme drafted with W. L. Mackenzie King — and a publicity campaign run by Ivy Lee, whose bulletins were later shown to the Commission to be inaccurate.

Foreign Relations of the United States 1928, volume II, carries a chapter titled "Good offices of the Department of State to protect the interests of the United Fruit Company in Colombia" — four telegrams between the Secretary of State and the Minister in Colombia, March to June 1928, months before the strike.
Roughly 25,000 workers in the Magdalena banana zone struck in November 1928. The demands were written contracts, a six-day week, an end to payment in company scrip, and medical care.

On 6 December 1928 Colombian troops under General Carlos Cortés Vargas fired on a crowd gathered at the railway station square in Ciénaga. The death toll has never been settled: official Colombian figures were in the dozens, U.S. legation dispatches reported far higher numbers, and estimates range from under fifty to more than a thousand.
Jorge Eliécer Gaitán’s 1929 debates in the Colombian Chamber of Representatives are the principal public reckoning; no U.S. or company officer faced any proceeding.

The U.S. telegrams establish that the State Department acted as the company’s standing advocate in Bogotá. They do not themselves prove a U.S. instruction to fire — say so plainly rather than implying it.

Blackwater guarded State Department personnel in Iraq under the Worldwide Personal Protective Services contract, a cost-reimbursement vehicle whose task orders ran to hundreds of millions of dollars; the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform took testimony from Erik Prince at a hearing titled "Blackwater USA" on 2 October 2007.
On 16 September 2007 Blackwater guards fired into traffic at Nisour Square in Baghdad, killing seventeen Iraqi civilians and wounding more.

Coalition Provisional Authority Order 17 had placed contractors outside Iraqi legal process, so the only available forum was American. The criminal case was dismissed by the District Court for the District of Columbia on 31 December 2009 (United States v. Slough) over the use of the guards’ compelled statements; the D.C. Circuit revived it, and convictions followed years later in United States v. Slatten.
The civil suits brought by victims’ families (Estate of Abtan v. Blackwater Lodge & Training Center) were settled; the four men convicted were pardoned by President Trump in December 2020.
Keep the sequence exact — dismissal, revival, conviction, pardon — and do not state a settlement figure.

plannedQueue.topic: Union Carbide Bhopal gas leak litigation

queries.q: Union Carbide gas plant disaster Bhopal

anchors: On the night of 2-3 December 1984 methyl isocyanate escaped from a plant operated by Union Carbide India Limited (UCIL) at Bhopal. The Second Circuit described it as "the most devastating industrial disaster in history--the deaths of over 2,000 persons and injuries of over 200,000".

UCIL was an Indian company: 50.9% of its stock was owned by Union Carbide Corporation (UCC), 22% was owned or controlled by the government of India, and the balance was held by roughly 23,500 Indian citizens. It ran 14 plants in India, employed over 9,000 Indian citizens, and was "managed and operated entirely by Indians in India".

Some 145 purported class actions were filed in US federal courts and assigned to the Southern District of New York. On 29 March 1985 India enacted the Bhopal Gas Leak Disaster (Processing of Claims) Act, giving the Union of India the exclusive right to represent the victims "in India or elsewhere".

Judge Keenan dismissed on forum non conveniens on 12 May 1986 (634 F. Supp. 842) on three conditions. The Second Circuit deleted two of them — the consent to enforcement of a final Indian judgment and the submission to Federal Rules discovery — and affirmed as modified.

By orders of 14 and 15 February 1989 the Supreme Court of India approved a settlement of "all litigations, claims, rights and liabilities related to and arising out of the [Bhopal] disaster", under which UCC and UCIL agreed to pay $470 million. On 22 December 1989, in Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India, that Court upheld the constitutional validity of the Bhopal Act and the Indian Government's exclusive authority to compromise all claims.

In 1993 the Second Circuit held in Bi v. Union Carbide that individual victims lacked standing to challenge the settlement negotiated between Union Carbide and India. Keep the claimants' grounds labelled as contentions, not findings, and do not state a per-victim figure: none was read.
The India Code page for the 1985 Act could not be opened (edge error), so the Act is described only as the two federal opinions describe it.

plannedQueue.topic: Smedley Butler war is a racket munitions profits
anchors: This node is the racket thesis and Butler's own testimony. The 1933 Business Plot is a different matter and is already dossiered as "DuPont, General Motors & The Business Plot Axis" (CC-1914-DUPONT_GM_1934). Do not re-narrate the plot here.

The Vinson-Trammell Act (Act of 27 March 1934, ch. 95, 48 Stat. 503, Public No. 135, H.R. 6604) required, as a condition of any naval vessel or aircraft contract, that the contractor agree to make a sworn report to the Secretary of the Navy on completion and "To pay into the Treasury profit ... in excess of 10 per centum of the total contract price". It also forbade subdividing contracts to evade the Act, opened the contractor's books to the Secretary of the Navy, the Secretary of the Treasury "and/or by a duly authorized committee of Congress", and required subcontractors to assent.

The Senate Special Committee on Investigation of the Munitions Industry (the Nye Committee) reported in 1935 on naval shipbuilding that the Navy's failure to use its own yards as a yardstick "has resulted in leaving the profits of the shipbuilders practically uncontrolled"; that the Vinson-Trammell bill "limiting profits to 11.1 percent of cost cannot be enforced without a huge police force of accountants"; and that the Navy's 1933 and 1934 adjusted-price contracts "resulted, in effect, in cost-plus contracts", found "more profitable than the war-time contracts when only a 10-percent profit over cost was allowed".

The two percentages are the same cap stated two ways: 10 percent of the contract price is 11.1 percent of the cost that makes up the other 90 percent. Say so rather than letting them look like a contradiction.

The committee also found the Navy "has never examined the underlying costs or profits of the private builders", "makes no pretense of doing this", has no staff for it, and that the figures the committee studied "were all news to it"; enforcement was left "to the Treasury to do after 3 years, after a job is done". Evidence before it showed 1933 contracts worth $130,000,000 to private shipbuilders.

Butler did not testify to the Nye Committee — two of its hearings volumes contain no occurrence of "Smedley". His own testimony that is on the record in this window is to the Senate Committee on Naval Affairs, on the 1914 "battle of El Tejar" near Veracruz: as recounted in the Senate on 5 March 1935, Butler testified that his troops reached the waterworks, made a reconnaissance and "could find no enemy", against General Russell's testimony of five or six hundred Mexicans and being shot at about twenty times. The chairman of that committee was Senator Park Trammell, whose name is on the 1934 profit cap. Do not stretch this into testimony about war profits; it is not.
No verifiable 1935 scan of the book "War Is a Racket" was found, so do not quote the book.

plannedQueue.topic: Standard Oil dissolution decree and oil-property diplomacy

queries.q: Standard Oil Company of New Jersey v United States

anchors: Standard Oil Co. of New Jersey v. United States, 221 U.S. 1 (1911), on appeal from the Circuit Court for the Eastern District of Missouri: argued 14-16 March 1910, restored to the docket for reargument 11 April 1910, reargued 12-17 January 1911, decided 15 May 1911. The Court construed the Sherman Act "in the light of reason" so that it prohibits only unreasonable or undue restraints, and held the combination an unreasonable restraint of trade in petroleum.

Paragraph 5 of the Circuit Court decree permitted "the distribution among the shareholders of the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey of the stocks held by that company" — the holding company was unwound into the hands of its own shareholders. This is recorded in the appellants' assignment of errors, which complained that the court then went on to limit the method of that distribution.

The Supreme Court modified the decree in two respects that matter: it held "the delay of thirty days allowed for executing the decree was too short and should be extended so as to embrace a period of at least six months", and it held that the paragraph 7 injunction — which would have enjoined the New Jersey corporation and all the subsidiaries from carrying on interstate commerce until the stocks were transferred — "should not have been awarded".

It construed paragraph 6 not as depriving the stockholders or corporations of the power "to make normal and lawful contracts or agreements", but "as restraining them from, by any device whatever, recreating directly or indirectly the illegal combination which the decree dissolved".

Justice Harlan concurred in the general affirmance but dissented from the modification and from the rule of reason, writing that the Court had "read into the act of Congress words which are not to be found there".

On 18 August 1914 William H. Libby, for the Standard Oil Company of New Jersey, wrote to the Secretary of State asking that the Government "secure the assent of the powers engaged in the present conflict to the exemption from seizure and inquiry of vessels transferred to the American flag which were actually owned in this country before the war began", citing the protection already accorded "the six American steamers of the International Mercantile Marine Company".

Do not assert post-1911 ownership percentages or that any particular person retained control: the record read here shows what the decree permitted, not who ended up holding what. There is no documented Standard Oil gunboat episode in 1914-15 Mexico — the FRUS 1915 "Protection of American oil interests" file contains no occurrence of "Standard Oil" — so make no such claim.

On 18 June 2023, about 1047 local time, while diving to the wreck of the Titanic about 372 miles southeast of St. John's, Newfoundland and Labrador, the submersible Titan's pressure hull failed and the vessel imploded. All five persons on board died.

The NTSB's Marine Investigation Report MIR-25-36 (investigation DCA23FM036) determines the probable cause to be "OceanGate's inadequate engineering process, which failed to establish the actual strength and durability of the Titan pressure vessel", with the hull having sustained delamination damage after dive 80 and further damage of unknown origin after dive 82, leading to a local buckling failure on dive 88. Contributing were "US and international voluntary guidance and US small passenger vessel regulations that were insufficient to ensure OceanGate adhered to established industry standards", and OceanGate's flawed analysis of its own pressure-vessel monitoring data.

Titan was owned by Cyclops II Inc and operated by OceanGate Expeditions, based in The Bahamas, both affiliates of OceanGate Inc. The NTSB records that "The Titan was not registered in any US state, documented by the US National Vessel Documentation Center, nor inspected by any flag state", with flag, port of registry, IMO number and classification society all recorded as not applicable. Built 2020.

OceanGate called its paying clients "mission specialists" — in the 2023 expedition's Project Execution Plan, "guests who help fund OceanGate" who were assigned tasks. A former operations technician told the chief executive "... you can't just change the title of a person when you're receiving compensation", and resigned citing "the legality of how it [OceanGate] was operating"; he also reported the CEO saying that "if the [US] Coast Guard became a problem ... he would buy himself a congressman and make it go away." The NTSB notes "OceanGate's intent to avoid safety oversight by assigning tasks to those paying to ride", while stating that it does not determine whether conduct violated statutory or regulatory requirements.

When the Coast Guard published NVIC 05-93 in 1993, submersibles carrying six or fewer passengers were treated as "uninspected" vessels rather than small passenger vessels; after the Passenger Vessel Safety Act of 1993 the definition changed to include any submersible carrying at least one passenger for hire. OceanGate did not register or document the Titan in the United States or arrange Coast Guard inspection. NVIC 05-93 recommended keeping submersible operations within the depth at which rescue assistance is effective; the Titan regularly dove far beyond it, generally without rescue assistance standing by.

The US Coast Guard Marine Board of Investigation released its Report of Investigation on 5 August 2025: more than 300 pages, 17 safety recommendations; chair Jason Neubauer said "This marine casualty and the loss of five lives was preventable." It found the primary contributing factors to be OceanGate's inadequate design, certification, maintenance and inspection process, and cited a toxic workplace culture, an inadequate regulatory framework and an ineffective whistleblower process under the Seaman's Protection Act. Its report was still under review by the Commandant, pending a Final Action Memorandum.

The ROI PDF itself is served behind a bot wall and was not read; the Coast Guard citation is the official press release. Neither board determines liability, and no finding of liability should be implied.
